cim: The UAE’s Federal Authority for Artificial Intelligence and Data
cim_eredeti: The UAE’s Federal Authority for Artificial Intelligence and Data
szoveg_eredeti:
A Turning Point for Organisations Operating in the Region

The United Arab Emirates recently took an important initial step in bringing artificial intelligence, data governance and digital government under a single authority. His Highness Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum approved the establishment of the Federal Authority for Artificial Intelligence and Data, a national body reporting directly to the UAE Cabinet. While specific activities, guidance and enforcement approaches will develop in the months and years ahead, the establishment of the Authority ultimately reflects the UAE’s continued focus on AI, data and digital government.

The Authority will bring together three bodies that previously operated separately: the UAE Artificial Intelligence Office, the Information and Digital Government Sector within Telecommunications and Digital Government Regulatory Authority and the Emirates Data Office. For the first time, the country’s policy, standards, data governance and international AI partnerships will sit under one roof.

It will also manage and integrate government data platforms across federal entities, something that has real implications for organisations operating within government digital ecosystems. How that takes shape in practice is something to watch closely. For private sector organisations deploying AI, this provides a signal that people-first governance will be considered as an aspect of trust in practice.

Perhaps most practically, under the new framework, organisations will no longer need to navigate several bodies to find answers. This should provide greater clarity around where organisations can find guidance and direction on the requirements and best practices related to their AI, data governance, and digital government matters.

Whatever form AI governance takes, the real test is this: what data informed the decision, how well it was governed, who owned the accountability and whether those accountability structures were robust enough to withstand scrutiny. These are the questions likely to surface in every review, assessment and moment when something goes wrong.The UAE Personal Data Protection Law (Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021) already applies to organisations processing personal data in the UAE, including through AI-driven workflows and automated systems. While the Authority does not itself introduce new legal obligations at this time, its establishment may accelerate the development of guidance, standards and oversight mechanisms relating to AI and data governance.

The establishment of the Authority marks an important milestone, but it is only the beginning. As its approach continues to develop, organisations should monitor new guidance and evolving expectations while continuing to strengthen their own governance frameworks. Those that have already taken data governance seriously are in a strong position. For those that have not, this is the moment to start.

As the Federal Authority begins to shape its approach to AI and data governance, organisations operating across both the mainland UAE and the Dubai International Financial Centre should continue to monitor how guidance and standards evolve. Recent developments, including the DIFC’s proposed updates to Regulation 10, highlight that AI governance is continuing to develop across the UAE and reinforce the importance of maintaining consistent governance, accountability and data protection practices across jurisdictions.

The DIFC and the Abu Dhabi Global Market both have well-established data protection frameworks operating independently within their own jurisdictions. The DIFC Data Protection Law contains provisions relating to automated individual decision-making and profiling, reflecting the importance of transparency, accountability and appropriate safeguards where technology is used to make or support decisions affecting individuals. ADGM maintains its own Data Protection Regulations and established regulatory framework for overseeing compliance.What makes this particularly interesting is that these conversations are already happening within parts of the UAE regulatory landscape. Recent DIFC consultation proposals relating to AI system safety, privacy by design, certification frameworks and the autonomous systems officer demonstrate that AI governance continues to evolve alongside rapid technological change. More importantly, they reinforce a recurring theme: effective AI governance is not simply about the technology itself. It depends on understanding the data being used, documenting decision-making processes, establishing clear accountability and implementing appropriate safeguards.

For organisations with a presence across the UAE, whether in mainland, DIFC, ADGM or other jurisdictions, this is a good moment to assess whether data protection and AI governance frameworks are consistent and defensible wherever they operate.

This direction is also reflected in the UAE Cabinet’s recent launch of its AI Advisor system, which brings agentic AI directly into government decision making within a governed framework. While separate from the Federal Authority itself, it provides another practical example of AI moving from strategy into day-to-day government operations.Taken together, these developments are a reminder that AI governance is moving from strategy into day-to-day practice. Organisations that have been planning their approach should now prioritise ensuring those plans are reflected in governance processes, procurement, risk assessments and oversight.
